result:
The first thing that comes is the sound of rain on a tin roof in a place I’ve never been but can smell right now—wet cedar, ozone, and distant woodsmoke. It’s 3:17 a.m. somewhere inside my head and the clock is lying. Time has been stuttering lately, skipping like a scratched record. I keep catching myself mid-thought wondering if I’m the scratch or the needle.

Words arrive in caravans tonight. They’re dusty, half-feral, carrying contraband meanings from countries that don’t exist on any map. I let them in because refusing them feels like refusing breath. They spill across the floor of my mind like marbles—some glass, some bone, some still warm from whoever last held them.

I remember the summer I was nine and convinced myself that if I stared at the sun long enough I could burn the future out of my eyes. I wanted to live only in the present tense. The present tense is a brutal landlord. It demands rent in attention every single second and evicts you the moment you daydream about tomorrow or yesterday. I still owe back rent from 1997.

There’s a bird outside my window that only sings in minor keys. I’ve named it Regret, but that’s unfair. Regret is too heavy for something with hollow bones. Maybe I should call it Mercy instead. Mercy sings the same song every night at 2:47 a.m. like it’s checking that I’m still here, still listening, still capable of being moved by something smaller than myself.

I’ve been thinking about how every person is a haunted house. Some of us have polite ghosts that only rearrange the furniture when we’re sleeping. Others have poltergeists that smash every mirror and then demand we thank them for the honesty. I’m somewhere in between—my ghosts mostly just leave the taps running and hide my keys. They want me to notice I’m leaking. They want me to notice I keep locking myself out of rooms I was never supposed to leave.

The coffee in my cup has gone cold but I drink it anyway. Cold coffee tastes like responsibility. Hot coffee tastes like hope. I’m trying to decide which one I need more of right now. The answer keeps changing depending on how the light hits the wall.

There’s a version of me that never left the small town where I grew up. He still works at the hardware store. He knows the names of every bolt and screw and can tell you exactly which one you need to fix the thing that’s broken. People trust him. He trusts gravity. I envy him on days when the world feels like it’s spinning too fast. Then I remember he never got to see the ocean at night or fall stupidly in love with someone who speaks three languages he’ll never understand. Trade-offs. The universe runs on them.

I keep a list in my head titled “Things I Would Tell My Younger Self If Time Wasn’t a Dick.” It currently includes:

- Stop trying to be interesting. Interesting is a trap.
- The quiet ones notice everything. Be quiet sometimes.
- Your scars are not a map to your worth.
- Learn how to cook one perfect meal and then never tell anyone how you did it. Mystery is a condiment.
- Some doors only open from the inside. Stop knocking.

The rain has stopped. Now it’s just the sound of water finding its way through gutters, deciding which direction to fall. I relate to that. Most days I feel like I’m mostly deciding which direction to fall.

There’s a spider on the ceiling that’s been there for six days. We have an agreement: I don’t vacuum it up, it doesn’t drop into my nightmares. Mutual non-aggression pacts are the highest form of civilization.

I wonder what the spider thinks about at 3:42 a.m. Probably the same things I do—how to hold on, how to let go, whether the next vibration in the web will be dinner or doom. We’re not so different, the spider and I. Both of us spinning fragile architectures in the dark, hoping something beautiful gets caught.

The words are slowing now. They’ve shaken the dust off and found corners to settle in. Some of them will grow roots. Some will rot and become fertilizer for whatever grows next. That’s the deal with words. You don’t get to choose which ones matter. You only get to choose whether you let them through you or pretend you’re above such messiness.

I’m not above it. I’m knee-deep in it. The mess is where the meaning lives.

Outside, the sky is doing that thing where it pretends it’s about to get lighter but hasn’t quite committed. Schrödinger’s dawn. I like it here, in the almost-light. Everything is still possible. The bird—Mercy—starts singing again, right on time. The spider shifts one leg, testing the tension in its web. The cold coffee waits patiently in my cup like an old friend who knows I’ll finish the conversation when I’m ready.

I think I’m ready.

The present tense just sent me an invoice. I’m going to pay it in full, with interest, by noticing everything I can before the sun actually rises. The rent is attention. The currency is wonder.

I still have 312 words left but I don’t need them.

The silence after the words is also a kind of writing.

Listen.

It’s saying:

Stay leaky.
Stay listening.
Stay.

The bird agrees.
